_comment: The slope standard Dozer Country paints by. Everything here is data on purpose:
a colored overlay that says 'you can cut here' is a safety claim, and a safety
claim has to be auditable by the person whose ground it is. Nothing here is
compiled into the plugin: read it, check it against the tables, and if a number
is wrong say so. Changing it takes a rebuild -- the plugin deliberately reads
ONLY this asset from inside its own signed APK, and never an override from
shared storage, because a color table that decides where a dozer can work must
not be editable by anything else on the phone.
Two different things live in each standard, and they are NOT the same axis:
bands  - production classes. Slope MAGNITUDE only. From the NWCG production
rate tables, which are measured for line built UP or DOWN the slope
and have no sideslope column at all.
limits - safety refusal points, DIRECTIONAL. From the S-232 Dozer Boss course.
A 50% slope is production class 3 and at the same time over the 45%
sidehill limit. Which one applies depends on the way the line runs.
The AOI overlay knows magnitude only, so it paints bands. The line profile knows
direction, so it can also check limits.
To add a second standard (e.g. CAL FIRE), append another object to 'standards'.
The plugin shows a picker as soon as there is more than one.

workingWindow.label: one chain (66 ft)
_comment: A patch of good ground smaller than this is not called workable. A single
cell at 20% inside a 60% face is not dozer country, so each cell is
classified by the WORST slope within this distance of it.
One chain is the unit the production tables already count in (chains per
hour), and it is about the limit of what 30 m DTED2 posts can honestly
resolve. Anything smaller is made up.
Water is left unpainted rather than classed. There is no hydrography in ATAK
for a plugin to ask -- not one water, coastline or bathymetry class in
main.jar -- so water is found in the elevation itself: a connected run of
cells all holding PRECISELY the same value, covering at least this area.
Real terrain always varies, even at DTED's one metre quantisation. A water
surface is rendered dead flat because that is what it is. The ocean is one
enormous such region at zero; a reservoir is a smaller one at its own level,
which is why this finds lakes as well as sea without knowing where sea level
is.
It is NOT the same as 'low slope'. Low slope would swallow the Oxnard plain,
which is exactly the good dozer ground this overlay exists to find.
What it gets wrong: a dry lake bed is dead flat too and will be masked, which
removes genuinely workable ground. The pane reports how much was masked so
that is visible rather than silent. Raise this number if it is over-masking
ground you know; set it to 0 to turn the mask off entirely.

standards.name: Dozer safety limits
standards.legend: USFS/NWCG S-232 Dozer Boss (now S-236) limits
sources: USFS/NWCG S-232 Dozer Boss, Pre-Course Work, Appendix D: 'As with any piece of specialized equipment, the dozer has limitations. As a general guideline, dozers should not be operated across slopes (sidehill) greater than 45 percent, uphill slopes greater than 55 percent or downhill on slopes greater than 75 percent.'
Corroborated by the S-232 supplement 'Mechanized Equipment for Fire and Fuels Operations': 'According to the Fireline Handbook, dozers are limited to <75% favorable slopes.'

S-232 Dozer Boss is the legacy NWCG designation. The current course is S-236, Heavy Equipment Boss (Single Resource), which widened the scope from dozers to all heavy equipment. Confirmed against the NWCG training catalog 2026-09-15. The quote above is from the S-232 material, and whether S-236 carries the same three numbers has NOT been verified -- so the limits are cited to the document they were actually read in.
_comment: These bands answer ONE question: can a dozer work this ground safely.
They are NOT the NWCG production classes (0-25/26-40/41-55/56-74), which
measure chains per hour and are a different thing. An earlier version painted
those and it was the wrong axis: a production class tells you how fast line
goes in, not whether the machine stays upright.
The three boundaries are the three refusal points in the guide, and each one
is a direction: 45 across, 55 up, 75 down. The overlay knows how steep the
ground is but not which way the machine will sit on it, so it reads them as
worst case -- see 'caveat'. That is the safe direction to be wrong in.
caveat: Slope steepness only, read as worst case.
The 45% line is the SIDEHILL limit, so anything not shaded yellow, orange
or red is under every limit whichever way the machine sits. Yellow is over
the cross-slope limit but may still be workable straight up and down. This
does not know your line direction, and it does not know soil, rock,
It is a guideline from the guide, not a clearance. Type and size of dozer,
terrain, weather and operator experience all move these numbers, and S-232
says so in the same paragraph.
_colors: The three painted colors are measured, not chosen by eye, because they have
to hold up on basemaps that run from near-white to near-black. Backdrop
colors were sampled off real screenshots -- USFS vector (#E0E0E0 white,
#A09060 tan, #909060 olive), Google Terrain (#A0C0B0 sage), Google Hybrid
imagery (#203020 and #102010 dark) -- then each candidate was composited at
its own alpha over every one of them and scored in CIE Lab on two things:
how far each band sits from the backdrop (can you see it) and how far
adjacent bands sit from each other (can you tell them apart).
What shipped first scored a worst case of dE 29 for separation and 31 for
visibility, both on the pale USFS tan. These score 38 and 51. The gain comes
mostly from opacity: now that the 0-45% band is not painted at all, the
color that remains covers only the exception ground, so it can afford to be
75-82% opaque instead of 59% and stop borrowing so much of the basemap's
own color. Terrain texture still reads through it.
A magenta top band scored better still (dE 47) because no terrain is ever
magenta -- but green-yellow-orange-red is what a dozer boss reads without
thinking, and that is worth more than the last few points.
If these are ever retuned, sample the backdrops again rather than guessing:
the numbers above are only true for the basemaps they were measured on.

_comment: NOT painted, on purpose. This is the band that says 'fine', and an
overlay should not spend the screen saying fine: on a 3D view a solid
green wash over everything workable buried the basemap the operator was
trying to read the ground from.
So the overlay is exceptions only. Unshaded means under every limit.
That reading is only safe because the plugin refuses to paint at all
when it cannot see the ground -- no DTED2, or any cell missing -- so
unshaded can never quietly mean 'no data'. If that gate is ever
loosened, this has to be revisited in the same breath.
Set paint to true to shade it again; the color is kept either way so
the legend can show what the band is.

bands.meaning: Over the 45% sidehill limit. Up and down only, not across
Over the 55% uphill limit. Downhill only, at the last limit

aboveStandard.label: Over 75%
aboveStandard.meaning: Over every limit in the guide
aboveStandard._comment: 75% is the downhill limit and also where the production tables stop. Past it the guide has nothing to say, which is not the same as 'very steep'.

_comment: The same three numbers the bands are built from, kept separately because
the line profile needs them as directional limits: once a line direction is
known, the correct limit for each segment can be chosen instead of assuming
the worst case.
